subject: Problems with interval-constrained latent variables, and a solution

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Problems with interval-constrained latent variables, and a solution
parts:
From time to time I need to deal with a model that involves a latent variable that is constrained to lie within an interval. For example, I am currently working with a model that has duration as an independent variable, but the duration is only known roughly -- I have upper and lower bounds on it.  I introduce a latent "duration" variable for each observation, constrained to lie within the bounds for that observation.

The problem is that these models always run excruciatingly slowly in Stan. On this current example it was taking so long that I had to dial down to only 100 iterations total (50 burnin, 50 sampling) just to get some sort of output I could look at to diagnose the problem. Those 100 iterations took 4814 seconds (72 minutes). Taking a look at the sampler parameters, I saw that n_leapfrog__ had an average value of 1454. Ouch!

Thinking about it for a bit, I realized what the problem is. If I understand correctly, HMC and NUTS work best when the curvature of the log probability density is nearly constant, as this means that the same step size is optimal in all parts of the posterior. But the transformation that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables -- inverse logit -- introduces a Jacobian adjustment term whose curvature varies wildly, from -1/2 when x=0 (where x is the unconstrained variable) and falling to 0 as |x| gets large (see attached image). If you have 23000 interval-constrained latent variables, this is a big problem.

The solution is to use the normal CDF to transform from the unconstrained to the constrained variable. Its derivative is the normal density, the log of that is a quadratic function, and the curvature of a quadratic function is constant -- perfect for HMC!

To be specific, I replaced

    parameters {
      vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] y0;
      ....
    }
    transformed parameters {
      vector[N] y;
      y <- lower_bound + (upper_bound - lower_bound) .* y0;
      ...
    }

with

    parameters {
      vector[N] x;
      ....
    }
    transformed parameters {
      vector[N] y;
      for (i in 1:N)
        y[i] <- lower_bound[i] + (upper_bound[i] - lower_bound[i]) * normal_cdf(x[i], 0, 1);
      ...
    }
    model {
      increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(x));
      ...
    }

The result: the time for those 100 iterations went down by a factor of 2.9 (!) and the average value for n_leap__ went down by a factor of 2.2, to 655.

This suggests that maybe the normal CDF instead of inverse logit should be the transform that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables.

Thanks! I'm hoping Michael will weigh in on this one.

I was just talking about doing some experiments with transforms
and efficiency yesterday.

I did verify your curvature calculation; Wolfram Alpha
even reproduced your plot as an added bonus:

http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=d%2Fdx+%28d+%28log+%28exp%28-x%29+%2F+%281+%2B+exp%28-x%29%29%5E2%29%29+%2F+dx%29

What I'd like to see is a basic empirical evaluation of these two
models:

parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
}
model {
}

and

parameters {
real theta_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
theta <- Phi(theta_raw);
}
model {
theta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
}

because that will isolate the effect of just the transform we
use. It's basically the difference between sampling from the logistic
distribution and the normal distribution.

The normal is nice in that its log density has constant curvature
for fixed sigma.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problems with interval-constrained latent variables, and a solution
parts:
Lemme explain what’s going on theoretically.

When we transform to an unconstrained scale the posterior density picks
up a Jacobian which manifests as a new contribution to the potential
energy in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.  When we use a logit transformation
this contribution is

V = log(1 + cosh(x)) + const,

which is essentially just a smoothed version of the Laplace distribution.
If we use the inverse-Phi transformation, on the other hand, we get
a quadratic potential,

V = 0.5 * x^{2} + const.

Now _both_ of these potential energies yield well-behaved trajectories
for HMC (HMC with either a static or dynamic integration time is
geometrically ergodic for both!).  The problem with the logit-induced
potential energy is that the period of the trajectory increases out in
the tails while the period of the inverse-Phi-induced trajectories is
constant.  What this means is that out in the tails the logit-induced
trajectories need to evolve for a much longer time to cover the same
distance, which is why the number of leapfrog steps increased 
relative to the inverse-Phi trajectories.

This is the general problem with heavy-tailed target distributions,
by the way.  As you get out in the tails the gradients get smaller
which causes the momenta to decrease and you need to integrate 
for longer and longer to explore each level set.  Eventually the
gradients get so weak that you’re not even guaranteed to come
back to the bulk (exactly when this happens is an open research
question).

Anyways, in a 1D problem where you have only the Jacobians
the inverse-Phi transformation is indeed expected to have better
performance.  Of course that’s not the typical situation in which
we’re in!  The original density will change the tails and wash
much of this behavior out, and in more than one dimension
chaos arises and things get even more complicated.  Then
there’s the computational issues of needing the inverse-Phi
function to handle initializations and the like.  

But if you have parameters with upper and lower bounds
and suspect that you might have consequent heavy tails
(you can also check this by plotting lp vs the number of leapfrog 
steps — if the number of leapfrog steps increases as lp decreases 
then you know that you have heavy tails) then it might be worth
trying the inverse-Phi transform instead of the default logit-transform.

theoretical knowhow to back it up) that the data would

On the other hand, without it, and without understanding it,
I don't know how people are supposed to understand what's
going on with the tools they're using.

I need a year to study manifolds!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Problems with interval-constrained latent variables, and a solution
parts:
For the case in question, I had only interval bounds on some durations that fed into a Poisson model. That is, I had something similar to

    x[i] ~ poisson(lambda * t[i]);

where the precise value of t[i] is not known. I had a simple model of the durations

    t[i] ~ exponential(theta);

and a known upper and lower bound for each t[i]. So, yes, the t[i] are weakly constrained within the interval. They are not, however, what I'm really interested in -- it's lambda that interests me. (This is all a simplification of the actual model, which is actually a multilevel Poisson regression.)

Those 100 iterations took 4814 seconds (72 minutes). Taking a look at the sampler parameters, I saw that n_leapfrog__ had an average value of 1454. Ouch!
>
> Thinking about it for a bit, I realized what the problem is. If I understand correctly, HMC and NUTS work best when the curvature of the log probability density is nearly constant, as this means that the same step size is optimal in all parts of the posterior. But the transformation that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables -- inverse logit -- introduces a Jacobian adjustment term whose curvature varies wildly, from -1/2 when x=0 (where x is the unconstrained variable) and falling to 0 as |x| gets large (see attached image). If you have 23000 interval-constrained latent variables, this is a big problem.
>
> The solution is to use the normal CDF to transform from the unconstrained to the constrained variable. Its derivative is the normal density, the log of that is a quadratic function, and the curvature of a quadratic function is constant -- perfect for HMC!
>
> To be specific, I replaced
>
>     parameters {
>       vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] y0;
>       ....
>     }
>     transformed parameters {
>       vector[N] y;
>       y <- lower_bound + (upper_bound - lower_bound) .* y0;
>       ...
>     }
>
> with
>
>     parameters {
>       vector[N] x;
>       ....
>     }
>     transformed parameters {
>       vector[N] y;
>       for (i in 1:N)
>         y[i] <- lower_bound[i] + (upper_bound[i] - lower_bound[i]) * normal_cdf(x[i], 0, 1);
>       ...
>     }
>     model {
>       increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(x));
>       ...
>     }
>
> The result: the time for those 100 iterations went down by a factor of 2.9 (!) and the average value for n_leap__ went down by a factor of 2.2, to 655.
>
> This suggests that maybe the normal CDF instead of inverse logit should be the transform that Stan uses for interval-constrained variables.
>
>
>
